The third test version of **NetSketch**. Its Wi-Fi model is now built on published measurements, traffic is simulated the way real apps behave, the problem list finds subtler trouble, and the phone app grows into a full Wi-Fi analyser.

> **Beta:** 120 automated tests run on Linux, Windows and macOS, plus the phone app's own checks. The new phone features were tried on an emulator, not yet on real phones: neighbours' networks, 802.11k/v/r, distance measuring and the long background watch need a real home to prove themselves. Please report anything odd under [Issues](https://github.com/NilsBriggen/netsketch/issues).

## Downloads

| File | For |
|---|---|
| `NetSketch-0.3.0-x64.msi` | **Windows 10/11**: installs NetSketch with a Start-menu entry, and `.netplan` files open in it |
| `NetSketch-0.3.0-x64-portable.exe` | Windows, without installing |
| `NetSketch-x86_64.AppImage` | **Linux** (x86-64, GTK 3): `chmod +x NetSketch-x86_64.AppImage`, then run it |
| `netsketch-macos-arm64.tar.gz` | **macOS** on Apple silicon: unpack and run `netsketch` |
| `NetSketch-Survey-0.3-beta.apk` | **Android 10+**: the companion app. It installs over 0.2-beta. |

The builds aren't code-signed:
- **Windows:** SmartScreen may say the publisher is unknown. Choose *More info → Run anyway*.
- **macOS:** if it refuses to open the app, run `xattr -d com.apple.quarantine netsketch` once.
- **Android:** allow installing apps from your browser or file manager when it asks.

## New on the desktop

**Traffic like the real thing**
- Every cable, Wi-Fi channel and the internet line's upload is shared fairly between the apps using it, with high-priority devices first. Devices on one Wi-Fi channel take turns, and slow, far-away ones use up more of the air.
- **Organic** traffic follows the time of day and how busy the household is; **Custom** lets you set each device's apps and an own load, to the internet or to another device (a backup to the NAS stays at home). You can change it while Simulate runs.
- In Simulate, apps come and go like real ones: a page loads when you click, a video fetches a few seconds at a time and fetches nonstop when the line is too slow, calls and games jitter.
- Moving dots show the traffic and grow with it; a cable's tag shows what flows now, on average, and what the apps want. A 24-hour chart shows the day.

**A Wi-Fi model built on measurements**
- Wall losses per band (2.4, 5 and 6 GHz) from ITU-R P.2040, 3GPP TR 38.901 and measurement studies. New materials: aerated concrete (Ytong), thin and thick brick, thick stone.
- Walls crossed at a slant cost what the physics says, not far more. A second wall of the same kind costs a little less.
- Signals bend round wall ends and corners, so doorways and halls matter, and the signal changes smoothly as you walk past them.
- Speeds follow the 802.11 table of data rates and the signal each needs.
- **How steady each link is:** frames resent, packets lost and how often it drops, from its fading (line of sight, antennas, channel width). Phones and laptops swing more because they're carried around. The device panel and the cable's tag show it.
- In Simulate a weak link really drops out and needs a moment to join again. Powerline slows down while a noisy appliance runs, and a microwave oven disturbs 2.4 GHz as strongly as real ones do.

**New checks**
- Your router and a loud neighbour both pick their channel automatically: they can land together or move back and forth. One click picks good channels and keeps them. It's a warning when the phone actually saw channel changes.
- A router on a radar (DFS) channel must move to channels 36–48 for 30 minutes when radar shows up; the check names the neighbours already there.
- An extender or mesh point repeating the worse uplink (one click moves it), and a repeater behind another repeater.
- Links that drop now and then, with how often.
- What the phone measured against the plan: a different channel, fast roaming on in the plan but off on the device, WPS left on, an extender's weak uplink measured right next to it.

## New in NetSketch Survey (Android)

- **Around you:** every network the phone hears, grouped by router: channel, width, standard, security, antennas, 802.11k/v/r, WPS, country, how busy it is, a signal history, and the distance in metres where both sides support Wi-Fi RTT.
- **Watch my Wi-Fi:** keeps running in the background (with a notification) for hours. Every second it records signal and router delay; it notes channel changes of your router and the neighbours', hand-overs, dropouts, delay spikes, loss bursts and signal dips, on a timeline for 10 minutes, an hour or a day.
- **Check-up:** the phone's own assistant. It covers crowded channels and the quietest one, routers jumping channels or chasing each other, sticky connections, extender and mesh uplinks, separate names per band, security, double NAT or a shared provider address, IPv6 and slow DNS.
- **Devices:** finds the devices on your network (UPnP, Bonjour, a quick knock on common ports), usually including your router's model.
- Each measuring point also stores a router ping and the link rates. Everything the phone found goes to NetSketch: the findings into the problem list, the watch log and devices into the phone panel.

**What a phone can't see:** which uplink an extender really uses (the app works it out from where each access point is loudest and how fast it is, and says it's a guess); other devices' hardware addresses; retry counters or raw packets without root. Android allows 4 scans every 2 minutes, so channel changes show up within about 40 seconds. Some details need Android 11 or 12.

## Known limits
- Signal bends round one corner at most; the loss behind a corner is capped at 20 dB because no indoor measurement of it exists. Aerated-concrete and stone-wall values are estimates.
- The coverage map shows the expected signal, not how far a real home may differ from it (typically 4–5 dB).
- The built-in browser shows simple pages only. macOS builds are for Apple silicon only.

NetSketch is free software under the **GPL-3.0**.
